title: 03. Databases & Data Modeling: Document Databases

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** A **document database** is a NoSQL store where each record is a self-describing **JSON-like document** (BSON in MongoDB, JSON in Couchbase/Firestore) with its own **per-document schema** — fields can vary across documents, nesting is first-class (arrays, sub-objects), and queries can reach into nested fields via **dot notation** (`user.address.city`), exemplified by **MongoDB** (the dominant open-source document DB, born 2009), **Couchbase** (JSON + SQL-like N1QL), and **Firebase Firestore** (managed, real-time), and used for **content management, user profiles, catalogs, event logs, and mobile backends** where the data is naturally hierarchical and the schema evolves rapidly.

Document databases sit between key-value stores (too simple — opaque blobs, no nested query) and relational databases (too rigid — fixed schema, normalization overhead). The data model is a document: a JSON object like `{"_id": 42, "name": "alice", "address": {"city": "NYC", "zip": "10001"}, "tags": ["admin", "vip"]}`. Each document is self-describing — the schema is in the data, not enforced by the database (until you add a JSON Schema validator). Documents are grouped into collections (MongoDB's analog of tables), but unlike tables, two documents in the same collection can have completely different fields. Queries use a JSON-based query language: `db.users.find({"address.city": "NYC", "age": {"$gt": 30}})` finds all users in NYC older than 30 — without a JOIN, without predefining columns, without migration. This flexibility is the central value proposition: the schema can evolve with the application, new fields can be added without ALTER TABLE, and heterogeneous data (blog posts vs. videos vs. galleries) can coexist in one collection. The trade-off: no joins (or limited — MongoDB has `$lookup` since 3.2 but it's not the primary model), transactions were single-document only until 4.0 (now multi-document ACID is supported with caveats), and schema discipline moves into application code.

MongoDB dominates the document database space and is worth understanding in detail. Storage: MongoDB uses **BSON** (Binary JSON) — a binary-encoded JSON with extra types (Date, ObjectId, Binary, Decimal128). Documents are stored in **collections**, which are stored in **databases**. Each document has an `_id` field (ObjectId by default — 12 bytes encoding timestamp + machine ID + PID + counter) which is the primary key and is automatically indexed. Indexing: MongoDB supports secondary indexes on any field, including nested fields (`address.city`) and array elements (`tags`), with B-tree indexes (default), geospatial indexes (2dsphere), text indexes (full-text search), and hashed indexes (for sharding). Compound indexes work like RDBMS (leftmost-prefix rule). Sharding: MongoDB shards by a **shard key** — `sh.shardCollection("db.users", {"user_id": "hashed"})` distributes documents across shards by hashing user_id. Choosing the shard key is the most important MongoDB design decision: it determines write distribution, query routing (queries without the shard key broadcast to all shards), and scaling trajectory (changing the shard key requires dump/restore — painful). Replication: MongoDB uses **replica sets** — a primary + N secondaries (async replication), with automatic failover via election (Raft-like) when the primary dies. Writes go to the primary; reads can go to secondaries (eventually consistent) or the primary (strong). Write concern (`w: 1`, `w: "majority"`, `w: 0`) controls durability vs. latency; read concern (`local`, `majority`, `linearizable`) controls consistency.

The other major document databases occupy useful niches. **Couchbase** evolved from CouchDB + Membase, combining a Memcached-compatible cache layer with a JSON document store, and adds **N1QL** — a SQL-like query language for JSON (`SELECT name FROM users WHERE address.city = 'NYC'`). Couchbase is popular in gaming, ad-tech, and telecom where low-latency reads + SQL familiarity matter. **Firebase Firestore** (Google, replacing the original Firebase Realtime Database) is a managed document database designed for mobile/web backends — real-time updates (clients subscribe to query results), offline-first sync, and tight integration with Firebase Auth and Cloud Functions. Firestore is huge in mobile app development (especially indie and startup) because it eliminates backend ops. **Amazon DocumentDB** is AWS's MongoDB-compatible managed service (Wire-protocol compatible, but internally different — built on Aurora storage, doesn't support all MongoDB features). **ArangoDB** is a multi-model DB (document + graph + key-value). When choosing: MongoDB for self-hosted or Atlas-managed with full feature set, Couchbase for SQL-on-JSON + caching, Firestore for mobile backends, DocumentDB for AWS-native MongoDB compatibility.

The killer use cases for document databases share a common shape: hierarchical/nested data, evolving schema, and access patterns that don't need complex joins. **Content management systems** are the canonical use — articles, pages, media items all have different fields (blog posts have body + tags, videos have duration + URL, galleries have image_list), and the schema evolves as the CMS adds features. Forcing this into a relational schema requires either a giant sparse table (mostly NULL columns) or EAV (entity-attribute-value) which is a query nightmare. **User profiles** are naturally document-shaped — name, email, addresses (multiple), preferences (nested key-value), social links (array). Different products have different profile shapes; a schemaless document lets each evolve independently. **Product catalogs** (e-commerce) — each product category has different attributes (laptops have RAM and CPU, books have author and ISBN, clothes have size and color). **Event logs and IoT** — each event is a JSON document with the relevant fields; MongoDB's flexible schema handles heterogeneous event types. **Mobile backends** — Firestore and Couchbase sync documents to mobile clients, handling offline use and conflict resolution. **Real-time analytics** — MongoDB's aggregation pipeline (a functional-style chain of $match, $group, $project, $sort stages) handles most analytics without a separate OLAP store. Real-world: **Adobe uses MongoDB** for Experience Manager CMS (one of the largest MongoDB deployments, handling content for Adobe's enterprise customers); **Uber used MongoDB** for trip data early on (and migrated to PostgreSQL — more on that below); **Expedia, eBay, Bosch, Toyota, Cisco** all run MongoDB at scale.

Real-world stories illuminate the trade-offs. **Adobe's MongoDB use** (Experience Manager CMS) is a success story: the document model fits hierarchical content perfectly (pages contain paragraphs contain text+images), the schemaless nature lets each customer customize their content model, and MongoDB's replica sets + sharding scale to Adobe's enterprise customer base. **Uber's MongoDB-to-PostgreSQL migration** (2014-2016, documented in their engineering blog) is the most-cited cautionary tale. Uber originally stored trip data in MongoDB, sharded by trip_id. The problems they hit: (1) **schemaless became schema-chaos** — different teams wrote different field names for the same concept (`trip_id` vs `tripId` vs `id`), and the schemaless DB accepted all of them; debugging required inspecting individual documents. (2) **Write performance** — MongoDB's per-document update + index maintenance was slower than PostgreSQL's columnar updates for their access pattern. (3) **No joins** — Uber needed to join trips with users, drivers, payments; in MongoDB this required multiple round-trips or denormalization, both painful. (4) **Schema changes** — without a schema, they couldn't confidently reason about what fields existed where. Uber migrated to PostgreSQL (with PostGIS for geo) and reported dramatic improvements: 4x lower write latency, simpler queries, and a clearer data model. The lesson isn't "MongoDB is bad" — it's that Uber's access pattern (relational, with frequent joins and a stable schema) was a poor fit for MongoDB's strengths (hierarchical, schema-evolving, no joins). MongoDB is excellent for its sweet spot; outside it, the trade-offs become liabilities.

The trade-offs of document databases deserve careful consideration. First, **no joins (or limited)** — MongoDB's `$lookup` is left-outer-join only and slower than RDBMS joins; for relational data, you denormalize (duplicate author into each article) or do app-level joins (multiple round-trips). Second, **transactions are limited** — MongoDB 4.0+ supports multi-document ACID transactions, but they're slower than single-document ops and have size limits; pre-4.0, only single-document atomicity. Third, **schemaless = schema-in-app-code** — without DB enforcement, bad data creeps in (typos, type drift, missing fields); mitigations include JSON Schema validators (MongoDB 3.6+), application-level validation (Pydantic, Marshmallow), and versioned documents (`schema_version: 2`). Fourth, **memory and storage** — JSON is verbose (field names repeated in every document), BSON less so but still bigger than columnar; MongoDB's WiredTiger storage compresses (snappy, zlib) but it's still bigger than a normalized RDBMS. Fifth, **index maintenance cost** — every index slows writes; MongoDB's index-on-any-field flexibility leads teams to over-index, hurting write throughput. Sixth, **operational complexity** — MongoDB replica set elections (10-30s failover), shard balancing, index builds (foreground blocks, background since 4.2), and the operational learning curve are real. Seventh, **aggregation pipeline limitations** — complex analytics still need a real OLAP store (ClickHouse, BigQuery). The decision framework: use document DBs when data is naturally hierarchical, schema evolves rapidly, joins are rare, and the team is comfortable managing schema in code. Use RDBMS when the data is relational, joins are frequent, strong consistency is critical, and the schema is stable. Many systems use both — PostgreSQL for the transactional core, MongoDB for content/event data, Redis for cache, Elasticsearch for search.

schema-chaos)"] Products -.->|"cautionary tale"| MIG ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` Document DB: JSON-like docs, per-doc schema, nested queries Collection "articles": +----+-----------------------------------------------------+ | _id| document (JSON/BSON) | +----+-----------------------------------------------------+ | 1 | {type:"blog", title:"...", body:"...", | | | tags:["tech","db"], author:{name:"alice", | | | id:42}, createdAt: ISODate("2024-01-15")} | +----+-----------------------------------------------------+ | 2 | {type:"video", title:"...", duration:300, | <- different | | url:"https://...", resolution:"1080p"} | schema! +----+-----------------------------------------------------+ | 3 | {type:"gallery", title:"...", images:[ | | | {url:"...", caption:"..."}, ...]} | +----+-----------------------------------------------------+ Query (MongoDB syntax): db.articles.find({ "type": "blog" }) // filter db.articles.find({ "author.name": "alice" }) // nested (dot) db.articles.find({ "tags": "tech" }) // array member db.articles.find({ "createdAt": { $gt: ISODate("2024") }})// range db.articles.find({ $or: [{type:"blog"}, {type:"video"}] })// boolean Aggregation pipeline (functional chain): db.articles.aggregate([ { $match: { type: "blog" } }, // filter { $group: { _id: "$author.name", // group by count: { $sum: 1 } } }, { $sort: { count: -1 } }, // sort desc { $limit: 10 } // top 10 ]) Indexing (B-tree, like RDBMS): db.articles.createIndex({ "address.city": 1 }) // single db.articles.createIndex({ city: 1, age: -1 }) // compound db.articles.createIndex({ tags: 1 }) // multikey (array) db.articles.createIndex({ "*": "text" }) // full-text db.articles.createIndex({ loc: "2dsphere" }) // geo Replica set (HA): Primary (writes) --async replicate--> Secondary 1 (reads) Secondary 2 (reads) Failover: primary dies -> election -> new primary (10-30s) Sharding (horizontal scale): shard key: { user_id: "hashed" } // distributes by hash +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+ | shard 1 | | shard 2 | | shard 3 | | range 0-5K| | 5K-10K | | 10K-16K | +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+ Query without shard key -> broadcast to all shards (scatter-gather) ``` ### Walkthrough 1. Each document is a self-describing JSON/BSON object. Documents in the same collection can have completely different fields — a blog, a video, and a gallery coexist without forcing a uniform schema. The schema lives in the data, not in DB metadata. This is the core flexibility: schema evolves with the application, new fields are added without ALTER TABLE, and heterogeneous data coexists. The cost: schema discipline moves to application code (Pydantic, JSON Schema validator) — without it, schema-chaos creeps in (different teams using `trip_id` vs `tripId` vs `id` for the same concept, as Uber discovered). 2. Queries use a JSON-based query language with operators (`$gt`, `$in`, `$or`, `$regex`) and dot notation for nested fields (`author.name`). The aggregation pipeline chains stages (`$match`, `$group`, `$sort`, `$project`, `$lookup`) like a functional pipeline — powerful for analytics but not as expressive as SQL. Indexes are B-tree (default), supporting single, compound (leftmost-prefix rule), multikey (array), text, geo, and hashed. Without an index, queries scan the whole collection (COLLSCAN) — slow on large datasets. Replica sets provide HA (primary + async secondaries, election on failure). Sharding distributes by a shard key — choosing the right key is critical. 3. Use document databases when the data is naturally hierarchical (CMS, profiles, catalogs), the schema evolves rapidly, joins are rare, and the team accepts schema-in-code discipline. Use RDBMS when the data is relational, joins are frequent, strong consistency is critical, and the schema is stable. The Uber MongoDB-to-PostgreSQL migration illustrates the trap: MongoDB is excellent in its sweet spot but a poor fit for relational, join-heavy workloads with stable schemas. Real-world success: Adobe Experience Manager CMS uses MongoDB for hierarchical content with per-customer schema flexibility — exactly the sweet spot.
